text:
nWave

nWave supplies specialist roles and a host-led delivery workflow for software teams. Its nwdes command builds one canonical handoff per feature — the single JSON record of the feature's facts — and renders briefs, role prompts, output schemas, and review packets from it. Your coding host (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OMP, Cursor, Copilot, or Devin) invokes the roles and runs the models; the root assistant — the session you talk to — runs verification and decides what happens next. You decide scope and trade-offs.

 Coming from 3.x? nWave 4 is a major release and a breaking change from 3.x. The old delivery runtime is removed, the 3.x delivery commands are replaced by the nwdes verbs, and Python 3.11 or newer is required. There is no converter for 3.x roadmaps or execution logs. Read the migration guide before you upgrade: 

New to the vocabulary? Each term below is defined at first use; the glossary collects them in one place.

 What is new in v4

- nwdes is the delivery tool. One canonical handoff per feature; briefs, prompts, schemas and packets are rendered from it. The host invokes the roles.
- The previous delivery runtime was removed from the source tree. nwave-ai install , nwdes and code-fact keep working.
- Python 3.11 or newer is required. pip and uv refuse the install on Python 3.10.
- Commit attribution is on by default (a Co-Authored-By: nWave trailer). An explicit off still wins.
- Jev is a per-project switch, decided at install or when a project is enabled. Jev, the remote judgment service for bounded questions, is authorized by default in nwdes . Installing nWave, or running nwave-ai project enable , on a terminal asks whether Jev may be used in that project and records the answer as "jev": "authorized" or "jev": "unauthorized" in the project's .nwave/config.json ; without a terminal the command writes the declared default and says so: "jev": "authorized" , or "jev": "unauthorized" when your machine-wide /.nwave/config.json refuses Jev. --jev unauthorized on a call refuses it for that call. The TYPESAFE API KEY environment variable is only a technical prerequisite: nwdes only checks that it is set and never reads, stores or logs its value. Configuring Jev shows how to set it. See PRIVACY.md.

Full notes and upgrade steps: release notes, What's new in v4, Migrate from 3.x.

 Install

Requires:

- Python 3.11 or newer;
- a supported coding host (see the table below);
- Git for commits — 2.38 or newer for the lane actions.
- Linux or macOS; on Windows, use WSL (installation guide).

Preview any install with --dry-run before it writes host files.

 

 --platform accepts exactly: auto , claude-code , opencode , codex , cursor , copilot , omp , devin , all . Auto-detect never guesses: with no detected host, the installer refuses before writing anything.

 Platform The installer deploys Verified by Guide 
 --- --- --- --- 
 claude-code Templates, utilities, agents, /nw- commands, skills, and settings.json (hook registrations) Container end-to-end install tests Installation guide 
 opencode Skills, agents, commands Container end-to-end install tests Installation guide 
 codex Skills, TOML agents, hook integration Container end-to-end install tests Installing for Codex 
 omp Skills, agents, /nw- commands, extension Installer self-validation Installing for OMP 
 cursor Global user hooks only Installer self-validation Installing for Cursor 
 copilot Hooks, public roles as custom agents, public skills; project-level agents, skills and prompt files on request (Copilot CLI only; VS Code and Visual Studio not tested) Installer self-validation, plus observations on the real CLI Installing for Copilot 
 devin Public skills under /.config/devin/skills/ plus a manifest Installer self-validation Installing for Devin 

Verification depth differs per host, as the table states: container end-to-end install tests exercise a full install in a container, while installer self-validation means the installer's own prerequisite checks and final validation report — no dedicated end-to-end test covers those hosts yet. Cursor is hook-only (no agents or native skills); Devin is skills-only; OMP receives skills, agents, commands and an extension; Copilot CLI receives hooks, the public skills and the public roles, with the observations listed in the vendor-support guide. Restart the host after installation, then confirm nwdes --help works — the one nwdes command you run at setup.

Installation is host-wide; project activation is separate and opt-in:

 

 project enable writes .nwave/config.json with "enabled": true and makes it trackable. Commit that file if your team should inherit the activation. Then, inside the host, ask /nw-buddy What should I do next? (Claude Code), $nw-buddy (Codex, OpenCode) or /nw-buddy (OMP installs the same /nw- commands). Cursor, Copilot and Devin have no host command: restart the host, then point your assistant at Deliver a feature — on Devin by asking about the installed nw- skills; on Cursor the assistant has no nWave skills, and on Copilot it does not find nWave by itself in a fresh session although the skills are installed, so paste it the sentence from For your assistant (the nwdes terminal route stays as a fallback there).

Before an upgrade you can create a recovery point with nwave-ai install --backup-only . nwave-ai install --restore rolls back a Claude Code installation; on Codex a restore is currently a no-op, and the other hosts differ — read the installation guide for your host's recovery surface. On Claude Code, nwave-ai doctor checks the installation; on the other hosts, read the installer's own final validation (doctor checks Claude Code assets, so a host-only install can fail it without being broken).

 First steps

The nwdes steps in these guides are your assistant's to run; the
For your assistant block gives you
the exact sentence to paste. The first lesson below is the one you type
yourself, once, to learn the command flow.

- First feature with nwdes
